question: According to Section 3.5 (Sorting Algorithms, page 127), how do Insertion Sort and Selection Sort compare in best-case versus worst-case time complexity, and why does Insertion Sort achieve O(N) best-case runtime on an already-sorted list?

tool_calls.query: According to Section 3.5 (Sorting Algorithms, page 127), how do Insertion Sort and Selection Sort compare in best-case versus worst-case time complexity, and why does Insertion Sort achieve O(N) best-case runtime on an already-sorted list?

answer: On page 127, Selection Sort always requires O(N^2) quadratic time in both the best case and worst case because it repeatedly scans the entire unsorted remainder to find the minimum element. Insertion Sort has an O(N^2) worst-case runtime (on a reverse-sorted list), but achieves an O(N) linear best-case runtime when the input list is already sorted (or nearly sorted) because each new element only needs a single comparison against its immediate left neighbor without shifting elements. question: According to Section 5.2 (Computer Levels of Abstraction, page 209), what three key characteristics must every algorithm have to be executable and useful on a computer, and why does an algorithm that counts all even numbers fail?

tool_calls.query: According to Section 5.2 (Computer Levels of Abstraction, page 209), what three key characteristics must every algorithm have to be executable and useful on a computer, and why does an algorithm that counts all even numbers fail?

answer: On page 209, every algorithm must have three key characteristics: (1) it must be unambiguous (each step is well-defined and precise), (2) it must be deterministic (reproducible and repeatable so the same inputs always produce the same output), and (3) it must be finite and consume a reasonable amount of time and storage (an algorithm taking 100 years is useless). An algorithm that counts all even numbers fails the finiteness/reasonable-time requirement because there are infinitely many even numbers. [openstax-ics-2024, p.209]
